Planning

ACS Central and Scanner V4 both embed PostgreSQL 15 as their internal database, and PostgreSQL 15 reaches end-of-life on *2027-11-13*. ACS must move both internal databases to PostgreSQL 16 before that date to stay on a supported stack. Central DB has a proven in-place {{pg_upgrade}} mechanism from the PG 13→15 migration (ROX-20769); Scanner V4 DB has *no* upgrade mechanism and one must be built. The single customer outcome: existing installs migrate to PG 16 transparently on upgrade, with no data loss and no scan downtime.

Central Upgrade and Rollback Version Bounds (N±3),ROX-36456,6870280,Project,To Do,ROX,Red Hat Advanced Cluster Security,software,Vu Le,6109c89c8ad5b60070efa19f,,Undefined,,David Shrewsberry,620a93c2a713ab0068114be7,David Shrewsberry,620a93c2a713ab0068114be7,David Shrewsberry,620a93c2a713ab0068114be7,2026/08/19 7:48 PM,2026/09/21 6:53 PM,2026/09/21 5:04 PM,,,,,0,,"The project [https://docs.google.com/document/d/1bOICrRv01FHyStNRh_WSDRt9ZRxAKJtxPvNojFUEOkk/edit?usp=sharing

ACS Central currently supports upgrading and rolling back across an unbounded range of minor versions. The migrator carries the full migration sequence history from 4.6 onward. This creates a compounding maintenance burden: old migrations must be preserved, old database objects (tables, columns, indexes) cannot be cleaned up, and upgrade testing must cover an ever-growing version matrix. Telemetry shows ~9% of Central installations are currently outside an N-3 version window, meaning this restriction affects a small but non-trivial number of deployments.

ROX-26374 (Closed) previously restricted rollback/restore to no earlier than 4.6, and ROX-33439 (Closed) revisited the upgrader refusal logic and CI checks for dropping old migrations. This project formalizes the N±3 policy, enforces it in the migrator, establishes a repeatable cleanup process, and addresses the Scanner V4 DB rollback gap.

column1: # The migrator rejects upgrades from versions older than N-3 with a clear, actionable error message (e.g., ""cannot upgrade from 4.4 to 5.2 — upgrade to 4.9 first"")
# The migrator does not crash-loop on a rejected upgrade — it exits cleanly with the error and does not retry
# A version-to-minimum-sequence-number mapping exists so the migrator can identify the source version in its error message
h3. Migration and DB cleanup process (ROX-36221)
# A documented, repeatable process exists for cleaning up old migrations after each release branch cut
# Old database objects (tables, columns, indexes) that are no longer reachable via rollback are removed
# Database snapshots for upgrade tests (stored in GCS) are updated to reflect the pruned state
# The cleanup process is executed for the current release (5.1.0)
# Release notes and upgrade documentation describe the N±3 restriction
# Documentation includes upgrade planning guidance for customers who need to cross more than 3 versions (stepping-stone upgrades)
# The exact migrator error message is referenced so customers can identify the issue
# A documented rollback path exists for Scanner V4 DB when Central's migrator blocks an upgrade but Scanner V4 has already started and migrated its own database
# The rollback path is validated in automated tests
# A negative test exists that verifies the migrator correctly blocks an out-of-range upgrade
# Previous version discovery is automated (handles version bumps and patch numbers)
# Upgrade tests automatically run in PRs when relevant migrator or migration code changes
# Rolling upgrades (spec.central.rolloutStrategy) are validated against the N±3 restriction with no breakage
# Any discovered breakage scenarios are documented with diagnosis and prevention steps for customers
* Changing the N±3 window size (this is the agreed policy per the decision doc)
* Migrating the ~9% of Centrals currently outside the N-3 window — they will need to stepping-stone upgrade on their own timeline

Planning

ACS policy management needs improvements across both its first\-use experience and the accuracy of policy criteria. Default System policies and probe\-policy behavior can create avoidable violation noise, while policy\-as\-code configuration and Dockerfile\-layer attribution leave customers with unclear or impractical controls. This project delivers targeted default\-experience and policy\-criterion improvements while preserving upgrade safety and limiting immutable\-label work to discovery.

Planning

ACS's compliance product loses customer trust in two ways today. First, scanning is incomplete and its state is invisible: when a Compliance Operator scan times out (~40 min) ACS silently deletes the cluster's results, and nodes in custom MachineConfigPools go unscanned entirely — so the dashboard shows misleading or absent data for a product auditors rely on (ROX-35712, ROX-34167). Second, once results exist customers cannot easily get them out for analysis or evidence — there is no per-node filter/export and no API-driven CSV export (ROX-34950, ROX-34898). A top-10 customer (OCBC) and multiple RFEs are driving this. The outcome: complete, trustworthy compliance scanning plus reporting/export a customer can hand an auditor.

Regulated and crypto-agility customers need centralized control over the TLS named groups/curves ACS negotiates — the {{groups}} field in OpenShift's {{TLSSecurityProfile}} — for FIPS/PQC readiness (ROX-34979, OCPSTRAT-3145). At the same time, the ACS operator must stay aligned with the target OpenShift platform (ROX-34570), and today its rollback path is broken: a failed upgrade rollback puts the operator in an infinite reconciliation/rollback loop that blocks manual CR fixes and, worse, wipes the service account's {{spec.secrets}} so OCP spawns thousands of secrets (ROX-31354, ROX-17688). The outcome: enterprise-ready, standards-compliant TLS configuration on a platform-aligned operator that fails gracefully.

column3: http://access.redhat.com/support/cases/#/case/04086122]). The central-db PVC — critical to Central — lives in a custom namespace ({{stackrox}} / {{rhacs-operator}}) that OpenShift's default PV monitoring doesn't cover, so it can fill and take Central down with no warning ([RFE-8250
column4: https://redhat.atlassian.net/browse/RFE-8250]). And exposing ACS custom metrics to OpenShift Prometheus still requires hand-built ServiceMonitors, API tokens, and auth workarounds ([RFE-9680
column6: https://access.redhat.com/solutions/7139236]). This project makes ACS observable and self-monitoring without manual setup.

Project Doc

Every StackRox PR runs the full CI pipeline regardless of what changed, resulting in ~75-85 non-skipped checks even for trivial changes like a CHANGELOG edit. This wastes compute, blocks developer velocity with multi-hour feedback loops, and creates noise that obscures real failures. This project introduces domain-aware test selection that maps changed files to relevant test suites, cutting PR checks to ~20-30 and wall-clock time to under one hour while maintaining full coverage on merge and nightly runs.
# A docs-only PR (e.g., CHANGELOG.md) completes CI in under 5 minutes with no tests or builds triggered
# A subsystem-scoped PR (e.g., sensor-only) runs only relevant BAT sub-tags, relevant Go E2E tests, and GKE + OCP latest — not the full pipeline
# A {{ci-run-all-tests}} label on any PR triggers the full pipeline, overriding all domain filtering
# Merge-to-master and nightly runs always execute the full test suite (unchanged from today)
# Unmatched files (not covered by any domain mapping) trigger a full run as a safety fallback
# A blocking CI check detects mapping drift — unmapped directories, missing sub-tags, stale job references
# Non-skipped checks per backend PR reduced from ~75-85 to ~20-30
# No increase in post-merge regression rate attributable to skipped PR-time tests
* CI infrastructure migration (Prow to GHA or vice versa)

The current node vulnerability data model uses shared edge tables (node_component_edges, node_component_cve_edges) that cause scan results for one node to impact results reported for other nodes. There is no node-scoped firstDetected timestamp — consumers must approximate vulnerability age using the CVE-level createdAt or the node's scanTime, both of which are inaccurate for per-node reporting. This is a data modeling problem analogous to what was fixed for images in ROX-25570 (image_cves_v2) and for VMs in ROX-32104.

A flat, denormalized node CVE schema (mirroring image_cves_v2) that eliminates cross-node interference, adds an immutable per-node firstDetected timestamp, and exposes it through updated endpoints with full search framework support. Includes a forward migration from the legacy edge tables.

*Stretch goal*: Expose node vulnerability data through a v2 gRPC/REST service, replacing the current GraphQL-only query surface. The new data access layer built for this project provides the foundation — the marginal cost of a gRPC service on top is incremental.

HA Central Worker: Remaining Periodic Jobs,ROX-36843,7031505,Project,To Do,ROX,Red Hat Advanced Cluster Security,software,Vu Le,6109c89c8ad5b60070efa19f,,Normal,,David Shrewsberry,620a93c2a713ab0068114be7,David Shrewsberry,620a93c2a713ab0068114be7,David Shrewsberry,620a93c2a713ab0068114be7,2026/09/08 11:59 AM,2026/09/17 3:35 PM,,,,,,0,5.1.0,"*Project Definition*

Currently, Central manages several background processes—including external backups, cert rotations, declarative config syncing, compliance reporting, and various data reprocessing cycles—within the same container as the API. This architecture increases the potential impact of failures, as any unstable job could disrupt API availability and data ingestion. Furthermore, it hinders the transition to a multi-replica Central model since these operations require singleton execution. Following the initial shift of pruning and reporting established in ROX-32705, this initiative aims to finalize the migration of all surviving periodic tasks into the dedicated central worker deployment.
* 1. External backup execution runs in the central worker deployment
* 2. Certificate rotation checks run in the worker deployment
* 3. Declarative config reconciler runs in the worker deployment
* 4. External data synchronization jobs (scanner defs, cloud sources, base image watcher, network graph external sources gatherer) run in the worker deployment
* 5. Compliance V2 report generation runs in the worker deployment
* 6. Reprocessing loops (image/node enrichment, risk reprocessing, platform component reprocessor, orchestrator CVE reconciliation) run in the worker deployment
* 7. Image/node enrichment reprocessing uses LISTEN/NOTIFY from Central to trigger on integration changes
* 8. Central's resource consumption is reduced and more consistent after job extraction
* 9. No functional regression — all periodic jobs produce the same outcomes as when running in Central

Project Doc

Central services are a single point of failure — the central pod runs as a single-replica deployment, so any pod failure, upgrade, or config change causes downtime affecting the Scan API, UI, alerting, and CI/CD pipelines. Recovery is slow due to in-memory caches that take multiple minutes to fill on startup. Central must support multiple active replicas so pod failures or rolling upgrades do not cause downtime.
# Central can run 2+ replicas configured via {{spec.central.replicas}} in the Central CR
# Single pod failure does not cause downtime for Scan API, UI, or Central APIs
# Rolling upgrades complete with no downtime
# Sensor connections load-balance and rebalance across replicas after failures or rollouts within a bounded time
# Delegated scans and CentralMsgToSensor route via headless service to the correct replica
# Tier 1 (hot path) caches synchronize across replicas without increasing startup time
# Tier 2 (low impact) caches are removed; Tier 3 (short-lived/per-replica) caches unchanged
# Operator sets default DB pool sizes based on replica count when unset
# No regressions in ACS when running multiple replicas
* HA for in-product single-pod databases — use BYODB for DB HA
* Horizontal autoscaling of Central replicas; replica count is static in the CR
* HA for secured cluster components (Sensor, Collector, Admission Controller)
* Performance and scalability work beyond multi-replica correctness

Problem Statement

RHACS tracks workloads exclusively through the ""Deployment"" abstraction. When a Deployment is deleted—or when the workload was never a durable Deployment (CronJobs, Jobs, pipelines, bare Pods)—all pod context is hard-deleted, images lose their deployment association, and users hit ""deployment not found"" dead-ends in violation and image views. Additionally, images are marked inactive based solely on deployment container references without checking whether pods are still running them, leading to premature pruning during rolling updates and for short-lived workloads.
# Pod records survive deployment deletion, retaining cluster, namespace, pod identity, and workload/controller type

# For images with CVEs or violations from Pods without a durable Deployment, the UI and API expose sufficient context to identify where the image ran: at minimum cluster, namespace, pod identity, workload/controller type, and image identity
# When a Deployment record is deleted, users can still retrieve historical pod context for related image violations instead of a ""deployment not found"" dead-end

RHACS can kill or scale down containers as enforcement actions when policy violations occur, but this destroys the container's runtime state — memory, open files, sockets, and filesystem changes — making post-incident forensic investigation difficult or impossible. Customers investigating security breaches need the container's state preserved at the moment of violation. Linux CRIU (Checkpoint Restore In Userspace) can capture this state transparently, but CRIU support in Kubernetes/OpenShift is still alpha-level and carries known limitations around storage, node-level kubelet access, and CRI-O compatibility.

Sensor's internal communication still mixes ad-hoc channels, direct calls, and partially migrated PubSub paths. This creates inconsistent cancellation, buffering, reconnect, and backpressure behavior. This project completes the migration and uses the common PubSub framework to establish predictable communication semantics across Sensor components.
1. In-scope Sensor components use PubSub instead of legacy internal channels or direct communication paths.
2. Message cancellation propagates correctly and stops current processing without stopping the component.
3. Each relevant queue has defined behavior during Central disconnect and reconnect.
4. Messages are retained, discarded, or reconstructed according to component needs rather than universally dropped.
5. Obsolete channels, bridges, and compatibility paths are removed after migration.
6. Tests cover cancellation, ordering, backpressure, shutdown, disconnect, and reconnect behavior.

7. Every migrated ProcessMessage path propagates cancellation to queued work. Automated tests verify that cancellation stops the current message while the component remains able to process subsequent messages.

8. Every affected PubSub queue has an explicit Central-disconnect policy. Automated reconnect tests verify that eligible messages survive and are processed after reconnection, while messages superseded by state synchronization are intentionally cleared.
